337.title: Not good to be alone (Genesis 2:18–25)
337.hook: the first not good in the Bible is loneliness
337.carry: bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh
337.howItsDone: Genesis 2 is among the readings some churches use at weddings, and some churches run visiting ministries for people who live alone, the housebound and the bereaved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Eden, a garden of delight given to the first human to work and to guard, and your line was tend and keep. What did you look after on purpose? Day three hundred thirty-seven.

Count the goods we've heard so far. Light, good. Land and sea, good. Plants, lights, sea creatures and birds, animals: good, good, good, good. Then everything at once, very good. Seven times, in the first chapter. And then, in the garden, for the first time, the story says the opposite. Not good. There's no sin yet. No serpent, no fruit, nobody has done anything wrong. The world is brand new. And still, something is not good. It isn't a flaw in the garden, or in the animals, or in the man. It's the man, by himself. Today is ezer, and the first not good in the Bible.
screen: `SEVEN TIMES, GOOD.` → `THEN, FOR THE FIRST TIME: NOT GOOD.` → `NOBODY HAS DONE ANYTHING WRONG.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him." Help meet. Two words in the old English, and they've caused a lot of confusion. Meet just means fitting, suitable, like the old phrase it is meet and right. So a help meet is a help that fits. Later, English ran the two words together into helpmeet, and even helpmate, and some readers heard a junior assistant. The Hebrew doesn't say that. The word for help is ezer, and elsewhere the Bible uses it for God. When a psalm says my help cometh from the LORD, the Hebrew word for help is this same family. Some readers put it this way: ezer is help from strength, not from below. And the second word means something like corresponding to him, facing him, a partner. Then the animals pass by, as we heard yesterday, and none of them is the one. So God puts the man into a deep sleep and builds a woman from his side. The Hebrew word often translated rib can also mean side, as in the side of a building. The man wakes up and speaks, and what comes out is a little poem: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." Some churches read this passage at weddings. But it reaches further than marriage. In the story, the first thing God calls not good is a person with no one beside them. Friends, family, neighbors: readers hear in it that people were made for each other.
screen: `HELP MEET: A HELP THAT FITS.` · `EZER: THE WORD USED FOR GOD.` · `BUILT FROM HIS SIDE.` · `THE MAN WAKES WITH A POEM.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT GOOD THAT THE MAN SHOULD BE ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone who's alone. Settle, and breathe. Let a face come to mind. Someone who lives by themselves, or lost a partner, or just moved to a new city. Someone who's quiet in the group chat. A neighbor you only see collecting the mail. Picture where they are right now, and what their evening might look like. Don't fix anything yet. Just keep them company in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. After the bell, decide how you'll reach out. The bell holds the time.
Ezer. The Hebrew word for help, used elsewhere for God's own help: the fitting partner God made for the man.
Your line: bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. Today, reach out to the person you thought of: a text, a call, a knock, an invitation to eat. Day three hundred thirty-seven.

it comes before any sin: a man, alone, in a brand-new garden.

options: nothing. the garden is complete.
a partner who fits him, someone beside him.

fork.reveal: none of the animals is the one. "it is not good that the man should be alone."

trapdoor: what you thought: the woman was made as an assistant.
what it means: a partner who fits, facing him, because being alone was the first thing called not good.
what a scholar hears: ezer kenegdo, a help corresponding to him; ezer is used elsewhere of God, and meet in old English means fitting.

338.title: The serpent's question (Genesis 3:1–7)
338.hook: did God really say? the fruit, the eyes opened, the fig leaves
338.howItsDone: Some churches read Genesis 3 on the first Sunday of Lent, beside the story of Jesus tempted in the wilderness, where he answers each temptation with words of scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first not good in the Bible, a person with no one beside them, and your line was bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. Who did you reach out to? Day three hundred thirty-eight.
screen: `BONE OF MY BONES, AND FLESH OF MY FLESH.`

segments.voice: The most dangerous sentences don't always sound like lies. Sometimes they sound like questions. Are you sure your friend meant it that way? Didn't your boss technically say you could? Is that really what the doctor told you? A good question opens a door. A twisted one leaves a crack of doubt in something you trusted, and walks away. In the garden, everything is good. Two people, side by side, naked and not ashamed. And then, in the third chapter, a new voice arrives. It doesn't start with a command, or a threat. It starts with a question.
screen: `A LIE CAN SOUND LIKE A QUESTION.` → `A CRACK OF DOUBT.` → `A NEW VOICE IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening in the King James Bible: "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" Look how clever that is. God had said: eat freely of every tree, except one. The serpent turns a whole garden of yes into a single no. And in Hebrew there's a pun. Subtil, crafty, is arum. One verse earlier, the man and woman were arummim, naked. Naked and crafty, side by side. The woman answers, and adds something God never said: neither shall ye touch it. Then the serpent says it plainly: "Ye shall not surely die." And the fruit looks good, and pleasant, and wise-making, and she eats, and gives some to her husband, who, the text says, was with her. Then: "the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons." Two things the story doesn't say. It never says apple. That came later; some think a Latin pun helped, since in Latin malum can mean apple, and malum can mean evil. And Genesis never names the serpent as Satan. Christian tradition came to read it that way, following the book of Revelation, which calls the devil that old serpent. Jewish tradition has its own readings of the story. Either way, the text shows how it began: not with a lie, but with a question that bent a good word.
screen: `A GARDEN OF YES BECOMES ONE NO.` · `ARUM AND ARUMMIM: CRAFTY, NAKED.` · `EYES OPENED, FIG LEAVES SEWN.` · `NO APPLE, NO NAME.` · then, large: `YEA, HATH GOD SAID?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a voice that twists good words. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days. Was there a voice, a headline, an ad, a comment, or the voice in your own head, that took something good and bent it into a question? You're not really loved. You can't actually trust them. Did they really mean it? Just notice it. Don't argue with it yet. Name it for what it is: a question that twists. If you pray, you can hold it up to God. The bell holds the time.
Arum. The Hebrew word for crafty, used for the serpent, and it sounds just like naked, arummim, one verse before.
Your line: did god really say? Today, when a voice twists something good into doubt, notice it, and go back to what was actually said. Day three hundred thirty-eight.

the text says the man was with the woman when she ate

fork.setup: the serpent asks: "yea, hath God said, ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" you're the woman. what's true?
options: God forbade every tree.
God said eat freely, except from one tree.
God never mentioned the trees.
fork.reveal: a whole garden of yes, with one no. the question's trick is to make the one no look like everything.

original.note: Hebrew: crafty, shrewd. It echoes arummim, naked, one verse before.

trapdoor: what you thought: the devil, disguised as a snake, tempted Eve with an apple.
what it means: a crafty voice asks a question that bends a good word, and trust cracks.
what a scholar hears: arum and arummim, a pun on crafty and naked; no apple and no Satan in Genesis itself; those come from later reading.

339.title: Where are you? (Genesis 3:8–13)
339.hook: God walks in the garden in the cool of the day, calling
339.howItsDone: Some Christians keep a daily examen or a habit of confession, an honest look at where they are before God, and some churches open worship with a prayer of confession said together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the serpent's question, and arum, crafty: a garden of yes bent into one no, and your line was did god really say? Did you catch a voice twisting something good? Day three hundred thirty-nine.

A house goes too quiet. A small child was making noise a minute ago, and now there's nothing. A parent walks down the hall and calls a name, and somewhere behind a door comes a tiny shuffle. The parent already knows roughly where the child is, and roughly what's happened, and calls anyway, because the point is for the child to come out. The fruit has been eaten. The fig leaves are sewn. Two people who were naked and not ashamed are now ashamed. And it's evening in the garden, and they hear footsteps.
screen: `A HOUSE GONE TOO QUIET.` → `CALLING ANYWAY.` → `FOOTSTEPS IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And they heard the voice of the LORD God walking in the garden in the cool of the day." The cool of the day: in Hebrew, the wind of the day, the evening breeze. It sounds like a habit, God out for an evening walk, as if this happened often. But this evening they hide among the trees. And then come the first words God speaks to a human after things go wrong. Not a sentence of judgment. A question: "Where art thou?" In Hebrew it's one word, ayekka. Where are you? Readers have long asked why God would need to ask. One old answer: God isn't asking for information. God is asking for them. It's a door left open, a chance to step out on their own. The man does answer, and his first words are painfully honest: "I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself." Afraid, naked, hid: three plain words, and no excuses yet. But the next questions go worse. Who told you? Did you eat? And now the blaming starts. The man: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree." Notice that: the woman, and the God who gave her. The woman: "The serpent beguiled me." Nobody says I did it. Some Christians read this scene as the start of a long story of God seeking people out. Jesus says it of himself in Luke: the Son of man came to seek and to save what was lost. And the question from the garden is today's word: where are you?
screen: `FOOTSTEPS IN THE COOL OF THE DAY.` · `AYEKKA: WHERE ARE YOU?` · `I WAS AFRAID, AND I HID.` · `THE BLAMING STARTS.` · then, large: `WHERE ART THOU?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: answer honestly, where are you? Settle, and breathe. Imagine hearing the question, not angry, just calling, the way you'd call a child who's gone quiet. Where are you? Don't give the polite answer. Give the true one. Tired. Hiding from something. Proud of something. Afraid. Doing better than last month. Notice if you start blaming. Let the answer be simple, a few words. If you pray, you can tell God where you are. The bell holds the time.
Ayekka. The one Hebrew word God calls into the garden, where are you, not for information, but as a call to come out.
Your line: afraid, and I hid myself. Today, when someone asks how you are, give one honest answer instead of the automatic one. Day three hundred thirty-nine.

they're a question: "where art thou?"
the cool of the day is, in Hebrew, the wind of the day
the evening breeze, when God is heard walking in the garden.

answer: "I was afraid, and I hid," then blame someone else.
come out and say: it was my fault.
fork.reveal: the man answers honestly at first, "I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself," then blames the woman, and the God who gave her.

original.note: Hebrew: where are you? One word, the first question God asks a human in the Bible.

trapdoor: what you thought: God was checking where Adam was hiding.
what it means: a call more than a question, a door left open for the one hiding to come out.
what a scholar hears: ayekka, where are you, asked in the ruach of the day, the evening breeze, as if God walking in the garden was a habit.

340.title: Clothes from God (Genesis 3:14–24)
340.hook: even as they leave the garden, God makes them clothes
340.howItsDone: Christians read the end of Genesis 3 in different ways: many Western churches teach original sin from it, Orthodox Christians often speak of ancestral sin, and across traditions the clothing verse is preached as a picture of God's care after failure.

segments.voice: Yesterday, footsteps in the cool of the day, and your line was afraid, and I hid myself. Did you give one honest answer instead of the automatic one? Day three hundred forty.

Two people are standing in aprons made of fig leaves. They sewed them themselves, in a hurry, on the afternoon everything went wrong. A fig leaf is big enough for the job, for about a day. Then it dries, splits and crumbles. Anyone who has patched a torn coat with tape knows the feeling: it holds, until it doesn't. That is what Adam and Eve are wearing when the consequences are spoken. The end of the garden story is full of hard words. Pain, sweat, thorns, dust. But tucked in among them, almost easy to miss, is one verse about sewing, and this time they are not the ones holding the needle.
screen: `AN APRON OF FIG LEAVES.` → `IT HOLDS, UNTIL IT DOESN'T.` → `ONE VERSE ABOUT SEWING.`

segments.voice: First the consequences, and they're heavy. The serpent will crawl on its belly. The woman will have pain in childbirth. The man will work cursed ground that brings up thorns. And then the line that many Christians hear on Ash Wednesday, in the King James Bible: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Notice who gets cursed, though. The serpent, and the ground. Not the man or the woman by name. And in the middle of the hard words, there's a line many Christians call the first gospel: God tells the serpent that the woman's offspring will bruise its head. Many Christians, from the early church on, have heard in it a promise of Jesus; Jewish readers have usually read it as the long struggle between people and evil. Then the man gives his wife a name. Eve, in Hebrew Chavah, which sounds like the word for living, because she was the mother of all living. He names her life, right after hearing about death. And then the verse: "Unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them." They had made themselves aprons of fig leaves, flimsy and new. God makes them something that lasts. God, the potter of chapter two, now a tailor. And only then do they leave the garden, with cherubim and a flaming sword guarding the way to the tree of life. The consequence stands. They don't go back. But they don't go out naked either. Many readers say this is the story's pattern from here on: real consequences, and mercy that goes with them.
screen: `THORNS, SWEAT, AND DUST.` · `THE FIRST GOSPEL?` · `EVE: THE MOTHER OF ALL LIVING.` · `COATS OF SKINS.` · then, large: `AND CLOTHED THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a kindness inside a consequence. Settle, and breathe. Think of a time something went wrong because of your own choice, and the consequence was real. A job lost, a friendship strained, a ticket, a scar. Now look again, more slowly. Was there a coat in the bag? Someone who showed up anyway. A word that came at the right time. A door that opened later. Don't rush it. Just look for one. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Chavah. The Hebrew name for Eve, sounding like living, given to her right after the man first hears about death.
Your line: mercy goes with them. Today, when you have to hold someone to a consequence, a child, a coworker, yourself, put one kindness in the bag. Day three hundred forty.

trapdoor: what you thought: the end of the garden story is all punishment.
what it means: real consequences, and inside them a mercy: God clothes them before they leave.
what a scholar hears: the serpent and the ground are cursed, not the people by name; Eve is named for life right after death is spoken; God the potter becomes a tailor.

341.title: Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:1–16)
341.hook: jealousy, a field, a killing, and the question: am I my brother's keeper?
341.howItsDone: Christians often hear the story of Cain and Abel as a call to responsibility for one another, and preachers turn to it when speaking about violence, jealousy and care for neighbors in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday, clothes from God, and Chavah's new name: coats of skins for two people leaving the garden, and your line was mercy goes with them. Where did you put a kindness in the bag? Day three hundred forty-one.

The first family outside the garden has two sons. Cain, the older, works the ground, like his father. Abel, the younger, keeps sheep. One day both bring an offering to God. Cain brings some of the fruit of the ground. Abel brings the firstborn of his flock, and the fat portions. And God, the story says, has respect for Abel and his offering, but not for Cain and his. Cain's face falls. He's furious. It's the heat of watching a brother get the praise you wanted. This story is about that heat, and what it does in a field.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, TWO OFFERINGS.` → `ONE IS RESPECTED.` → `CAIN'S FACE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Why was Abel's offering accepted and Cain's not? Genesis doesn't say. Readers have guessed. Abel gave the firstborn, the best. Cain's heart was wrong. The letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith. But the text itself is quiet. What it does record is God speaking to Cain before anything happens, in the King James Bible: "If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door." Sin, crouching at the door like an animal, and God adds: you must rule over it. Cain still has a choice. Then Cain talks with his brother in the field, and kills him. And God comes with a question again, the way he did in the garden: "Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?" Keeper. In Hebrew, shomer, from shamar, the same root as the garden: to keep, to guard. Adam was put in the garden to keep it. Cain refuses to keep his brother. And God answers: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto me from the ground." Abel never speaks in the story. Not one word. Even his name, Hevel, is the Hebrew word for breath, or vapor. But his blood speaks. Then the surprise: Cain is sent away to wander, and he's afraid someone will kill him, so God puts a mark on him. Not a brand of shame. A protection. Even the killer isn't left without care. Christian preachers have answered Cain's question for him, and today's line takes their answer: yes, you are.
screen: `WHY ABEL'S? THE TEXT IS QUIET.` · `SIN CROUCHING AT THE DOOR.` · `SHOMER: KEEPER, LIKE THE GARDEN.` · `THE MARK OF CAIN PROTECTS.` · then, large: `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check on a brother or sister. Settle, and breathe. Think of a sibling, if you have one, or someone who's been like one: a cousin, an old roommate, a friend from way back. Notice what you feel when you picture them. Warmth, distance, an old jealousy, an argument you never finished. Don't fix it now. Just hold them in mind, and find one real question you could ask them, something better than how's it going. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Hevel. Abel's Hebrew name, meaning breath or vapor: he never speaks in the story, but his blood cries out from the ground.
Your line: you are your brother's keeper. Today, check on one brother or sister, by blood or by choice: a text, a call, a real question. Day three hundred forty-one.

what a scholar hears: shomer, keeper, from the same root as Adam's job to keep the garden; and Abel, Hevel, a breath, silent, whose blood speaks.

342.title: Who was Cain's wife? (Genesis 4:16–5:27)
342.hook: the questions kids ask about Genesis: who Cain married, nine-hundred-year lives, and where the dinosaurs went
342.howItsDone: Christians answer questions like Cain's wife in different ways: many follow the old view that Adam and Eve had other children, and others read Genesis as a story of beginnings that doesn't name everyone. Churches differ on reading the ages and the days of creation literally.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cain and Abel, Hevel, and your line: you are your brother's keeper. Did you check on a brother or sister? Today, the question every Sunday school gets sooner or later. Day three hundred forty-two.

A Sunday school classroom: a felt board, juice boxes, a teacher who has just finished Cain and Abel. One brother killed, the other sent away. And a seven-year-old's hand goes up. But who did Cain marry? Weren't they the only people? The teacher smiles, a little stuck. Kids ask the best questions about Genesis. Who did Cain marry? Did people really live nine hundred years? Where are the dinosaurs? They often get waved away, and that's a shame, because they're good questions. Today, the verses right after yesterday's story, and the questions kids actually ask.
screen: `A HAND GOES UP.` → `WHO DID CAIN MARRY?` → `GOOD QUESTIONS, OFTEN WAVED AWAY.`

segments.voice: Genesis says, in the King James Bible: "And Cain went out from the presence of the LORD, and dwelt in the land of Nod, on the east of Eden. And Cain knew his wife." That's all. Nod is Hebrew for wandering, so the wanderer settles in Wander-land. Then a wife, a son, and a city. Readers have answered the puzzle in two main ways. The oldest: Adam and Eve had more children. The next chapter says Adam "begat sons and daughters." So Cain married a sister. An ancient Jewish book, Jubilees, even names her: Awan. Augustine agreed that at the very start it had to be so. Other readers notice that Cain fears "every one that findeth me shall slay me," and then builds a city. Who is everyone? They read Genesis as a story of beginnings, not a census, so other people are simply there in the background. The long lives get read in more than one way too: "all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty and nine years." Some take the numbers literally. Others note that ancient lists from Mesopotamia give their early kings reigns of thousands of years, and hear Genesis speaking in that style. And dinosaurs? The Bible never mentions them. Many churches, Catholic, Orthodox and many Protestant, see no conflict with a very old earth; others read the days of creation literally. And tucked into that same family tree, one man gets a single quiet line: "Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him." Genesis keeps its mysteries short, and leaves room for the questions.
screen: `THE LAND OF NOD.` · `SONS AND DAUGHTERS.` · `NINE HUNDRED SIXTY AND NINE.` · `ENOCH WALKED WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a question be welcome. Settle, and breathe. Bring back one question about the Bible, or about faith, that you once asked and got waved away, or never asked at all. Say it to yourself plainly. Don't answer it. Just let it sit in the room, the way Genesis lets its mysteries sit. If you pray, you can bring it to God as a question, not a test. If you don't, simply notice that asking it didn't break anything. The bell holds the time.
Nod. Hebrew for wandering: the land east of Eden where Cain settled, married and built a city.
Your line: good questions are welcome here. The seven-year-old's hand was right to go up. Day three hundred forty-two.

343.title: Noah builds (Genesis 6:5–22)
343.hook: in a violent world, one man builds a boat on dry land
343.howItsDone: Christians often see Noah as a model of faithful obedience, and early Christian writers used the ark as a picture of the church and of baptism, carrying people safely through the water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the land of Nod, Cain's wife and the questions kids ask, and Enoch, who walked with God. Your line was good questions are welcome here. Which old question came back? Day three hundred forty-three, the end of the week.

Somewhere right now, someone is working on a thing nobody around them believes in. A novel in a drawer. A garden in a vacant lot. A small business with three customers. A recovery, ninety days in. The neighbors raise an eyebrow. Friends ask, gently, how long you're going to keep at that. In Genesis, the world after the garden goes from bad to worse. One murder becomes many. And in the middle of it, one man is handed a set of building plans for something enormous, for a disaster nobody can see coming. Today's word is what he builds.
screen: `A THING NOBODY BELIEVES IN.` → `THE WORLD GOES FROM BAD TO WORSE.` → `ONE MAN, A SET OF PLANS.`

segments.voice: Chapter six opens with grief. God sees that the wickedness of humans is great, and the text says it grieved him at his heart. Then the diagnosis, in the King James Bible: "the earth was filled with violence." The Hebrew word for violence there is chamas: brutality, wrong done to others. But one verse cuts across the darkness: "But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD." Noah, we're told, was a just man, and he walked with God, the same phrase we heard for Enoch yesterday. So God gives him plans. An ark of gopher wood, nobody's quite sure what tree that is, three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high. A building, lying on its side. And the Hebrew word for ark, tevah, isn't the usual word for a ship. It means something like a box, a chest. The same word turns up again in Exodus, for the little basket of reeds that carries baby Moses on the Nile. Two boxes, one huge and one tiny, each carrying the future through deadly water. Popular retellings add crowds of neighbors mocking him. Genesis doesn't. A later New Testament letter calls Noah a preacher of righteousness, but the chapter itself gives him no lines at all. Noah never says a word until after the flood. What it records is this: "Thus did Noah; according to all that God commanded him, so did he." That's the week's last step: from a person alone, a twisting question, a call to come out, clothes for the road, a brother to keep, a slow walk, to a man who just builds.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep going on one thing others doubt. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you're building that not everyone believes in. A habit, a project, a relationship, a change. Picture it as it is right now: half-finished, a frame of boards on dry land. Notice the doubts, other people's and your own. Then picture the next plank. Just one. What is the next small thing you'd do on it, today or tomorrow? If you pray, you can offer it to God. The bell holds the time.
Ark. Tevah in Hebrew, a box or chest. The huge boat Noah builds, and the same word as the tiny basket that carries baby Moses.
Your line: build anyway. Today, put in one plank on the thing others doubt, even ten minutes, even if nobody sees. Day three hundred forty-three.
